utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. A few remarks before we start. First of all, I do understand that the parties would prefer to have the cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would just like to say I have no objection. But, Your Honour, I was just told that. It wasn't a preference. But, Your Honour, I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just don't want it to be thought that I contributed to that decision. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither has the Chamber, so therefore we'll first start with Mr. Bjelobrk. As far as the issue, we briefly discussed in relation to Mr. Prstojevic in relation to the possibility of prior inconsistent statements are concerned, I -- it certainly assisted me to get better aware of the latest developments, at least until a couple of weeks ago, in the decision taken by the Limaj Chamber, which is well-balanced common civil law Chamber, where some developments in English law, Australia law are mentioned. At the same time, the Chamber took the position that the statement of -- at least, the transcripts of the interviews of Mr. Prstojevic are not in evidence, so there might not be any need since the parts on which he was examined and where small portions were quoted might be such that there's no real inconsistency, so that therefore one would not have to decide. And it may go without saying that such a situation of inconsistency between statement and testimony, of course, should be clear from the beginning. That means that since the transcripts of the interview have not been tendered into evidence, that -- well, the appropriate moment to do that would have been at the beginning of the testimony of Mr. Prstojevic. So therefore it might not be a real problem. Then the Chamber received a list of exhibits rather late, I must say. The Chamber asked for it in time, and granted a short delay, but received it only late yesterday, in the afternoon, and the list is not entirely clear as far -- especially not in view of the numbering. It might be that it's reference to pages, but it's totally unclear to the Chamber at this moment what it actually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I help on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope Your Honours are going to see that in practice -- and I certainly throughout this phase of the case, as always, I adopt a pragmatic approach, though, of course, it's my obligation to comply with directions of the Trial Chamber. But I hope Your Honours will see that there isn't going to be a major problem that will emerge in this area this morning. It's my optimistic expectation that so far as documentation is concerned, we shall get through Mr. Bjelobrk's evidence this morning without any major difficulty or hitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are aware that the Chamber granted one hour and a half for cross-examination, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have not forgotten that one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also take it because the situation has changed a little bit since then, since Mr. Krajisnik is allowed to ask any additional questions, I took it that he was the one who would have suggested the exhibits to be tendered so that it would be to a great extent already in your cross-examination, Mr. Stewart. At the same time, looking at the list, there's a lot of books and newspapers. I think there's no need to remind the parties that although now and then books and newspapers assist the Chamber in reaching determinations it will have to reach, that this is not a trial which is conducted on the basis of media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say that -- that reminder to the parties, of course, is a wide phrase. So far as such a reminder to counsel is concerned, I doubt that Your Honour is not preaching to the converted there. You do not see me surrounded by books and articles this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I just noticed that that was a newspaper. But, of course, we have -- since we received it only yesterday rather late and we have no copies, so I could not even express any further opinion apart from that -- I wouldn't say it's scaring, but it's raising some concern if too much of the exhibits come from the media and not from the original source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to say, in fact, the word I was going to -- was going through my head then. I do understand that the list when received by the Trial Chamber and indeed the Prosecution might have been disconcerting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm inviting Your Honours not to be too disconcerted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Until you see where we actually go this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The best way to find out is to get Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Usher, could you -- or Mr. Usher. I don't know who to address. Could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're -- we're facing, as we so frequently do, the practical difficulties of printers and photocopiers breaking down. If there's any way in which support can be given in a constant problem that faces Defence counsel and the ADC in this area, I'm sure all my colleagues in other cases and in our case would be incredibly grateful, Your Honour. It's a constant bug there for our case managers and everybody else. Our team of monks doing illuminated manuscripts is not available this morning as a substitute, Your Honour, and we need that machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Is there any specific issue that -- I mean, you asked for our assistance, but can I do anything at this moment for you, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not -- not right this second, Your Honour. Your Honour made an offer to do photocopying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- which was very kind, but we didn't need to take you up on that, with respect. Your Honour, as a general point, the Trial Chamber has often indicated that it would do what it could behind and in front of the scenes to assist. And I -- I'm really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there's a general problem in - -

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is a big problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in functioning machinery for photocopying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is a big problem, Your Honour. We are faced with it constantly. Daily almost, I think is fair, Mr. Karganovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll call for specific attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, since it is quite some time ago, I'd prefer that you'd repeat your solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you now by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelobrk. Please be seated. Mr. Stewart will continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, good morning again. Mr. Bjelobrk, one of the points that you made in your evidence sometime ago was that Mr. Krajisnik was, in your opinion, a master of obstruction so far as the work of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly was concerned. You recall that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave -- and the page reference to the transcript is 8253 and then some following pages through to about 8260, for everybody's note. But you gave a specific example, which I don't want to go over again in painful detail, Mr. Bjelobrk, about Mr. Krajisnik, whether a resolution from your party should or shouldn't have gone on the agenda, and you, Mr. Krajisnik, supported it and then didn't support it and so on. You know the issue that I'm talking about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- and part of the problem, from your point of view and perhaps from everybody's point of view, was that SDS and SDP deputies at one point walked out of the session in June 1991, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Krajisnik appealed both to the SDS deputies and to the SDP deputies to return to the session?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can just try to remember that. Even if that was so, I didn't really feel that that was something very convincing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, at page 8259 of the transcript - and this was on the 10th of November - one of the reasons I'm not going over all this ground again, Mr. Bjelobrk, is just to remind you that His Honour Judge Orie did explore these matters with you in some detail. But it ended up with His Honour saying, line 20, at 8259, "Do I understand you well that the obstruction demonstrated here by Mr. Krajisnik consisted of not taking, as you thought it would be, the wise position to encourage the SDS representatives to stay in the Assembly meeting?" And your answer was, "Yes." His Honour said, "Thank you." And we then moved on to a different topic. So, Mr. Bjelobrk, is the position that you simply don't know whether on some occasion at which you were not present Mr. Krajisnik did or did not encourage SDS representatives to return to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I thought about that, I would get into an area of speculation. The work of the Assembly is public, so my views are based on what happens publicly at the Assembly. What happened behind closed doors would then be subject of speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, therefore I would invite you just very specifically to answer my specific question. Is it the position you don't know whether Mr. Krajisnik did or did not encourage the SDS representatives to return to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not do that at the speakers platform of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bjelobrk, you were a parliamentarian. Do you accept that the most likely effective way for Mr. Krajisnik to have encouraged the SDS deputies to return to the session would have been to do that encouragement outside the public forum of the Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it is that important which method you choose if you are responsible for the successful work of an Assembly session, which method you use, would you do that in a kind of behind-the-scenes lobbying or publicly. The important thing is to exert influence so that the Assembly functions in its full composition. The fact is that this did not happen. Everything else to me seems to be less relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry too much, Mr. Bjelobrk, about what seems relevant to -- to you, please. Is the -- is the position this, then, two elements -- one question but two elements: You -- you say you know that Mr. Krajisnik didn't offer any such encouragement publicly, but is it secondly correct that you don't know whether or not he offered any such encouragement privately?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I would like to ask for your understanding. The Assembly functions in a public manner, so there's no need for any kind of private estimates or lines of work in order to implement one's duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you're expressing now an opinion on what's the proper way to exercise the function Mr. Krajisnik held. You were not asked for such an opinion. I think it became rather clear from your answer that you say, "I'm not aware of any encouragement Mr. Krajisnik gave. He certainly did not do it publicly." And I also do understand that you have no knowledge on what he may have done privately in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. And I try as a witness not to go into that at all because this is impossible to know. I mean, I don't know what you did last night, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Bjelobrk. Thank you, Your Honour. You also - and this is at paragraph 53 of your statement which is in evidence. You said, "In my work in the Assembly, I drew the conclusion that Krajisnik was consulted by the deputies of the SDS about all issues. Whenever disputes were likely to arise in the parliament, the deputies of the SDS would address Krajisnik for an answer." Now, first of all, Mr. Bjelobrk, what is conceivably wrong or objectionable about that position?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything in that sense. I'm just stating that that is the way in which I think that that particular person demonstrated his authority. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't suggest anything inappropriate about Mr. Krajisnik's behaviour in that area or the deputies' behaviour in that area.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 53, which you refer to, I did not want to be judgemental. I was just stating the facts as I remember them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- there was a -- well, there were deputies' clubs, weren't there, of -- there were eight different deputies' clubs at the time. Do you recall that? In -- in the connection with the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to -- just to reel them off, one was the SDS and the SPO combined. I'll go through the list and then tell me if there's anything wrong with it. Secondly, the HDZ; thirdly, not in order of priority or anything, SDA; fourthly, Liberal Party; fifthly, MBO; sixthly, SDP. And actually I only end up with seven, I'm afraid, but Reform Forces Club. But all those deputies' clubs existed, in your recollection, did they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I -- we've probably been over this before, but I -- can we take it that on no occasion did you attend a meeting of the deputies' club of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have any reason -- any basis to dispute the proposition that the SDS deputies' club sessions were always chaired either by the president of the SDS, who was Dr. Karadzic, or by Mr. Vojislav Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the SDS club functioned from the inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have no -- you have no basis of which -- whether you accept it or not, you have no basis on which you can dispute that proposition.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to repeat your assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, wasn't it implicit in the previous answer of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm happy with that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- do you remember -- and I'm not going to take you to minutes on this; they're all checkable somewhere. But do you remember, Mr. Bjelobrk, that from time to time the president of the SDS deputies' club - that was Mr. Maksimovic - would during Assembly sessions ask for breaks to consult his deputies?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge, Mr. Bjelobrk, of pressures on Mr. Krajisnik, as the working president of the Assembly, which often prevented him from being able to attend SDS deputies' club sessions during those breaks?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that Mr. Krajisnik was indeed absent from the meetings of the deputies' club of his party, but I do not think that the frequency of his absense from those meetings was that high, for instance, out of the ten meetings that might have taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Bjelobrk, do you agree it's clear that when the president of the SDS deputies' club, Mr. Maksimovic, has asked for a break in the Assembly session to consult his deputies, that those are relatively informal meetings of the SDS deputies' club convened at -- by definition, at very short notice?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule - and this applies to the operation of any parliament worldwide - these usually are meetings convened at short notice. At least, that is how I understand it. However, my experience from that period shows that very frequently the meetings of the deputies' clubs were used oftentimes as a way of obstructing the work of the parliament because the head of the deputies' club of a given party, after the meeting was convened, needs to inform the parliamentary session why the work of the session was brought to a halt because of such a meeting. However, the practice at the time was that after such meetings were convened at short notice, the parliament would not at all be informed as to the reason why its session had been interrupted, and this was indicative of the work of the parliament at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, may I simply observe, with respect, that although you certainly did answer my question, what you said contained quite a lot that was simply not an answer to my question and -- and went beyond it. If we could keep as closely as possible to the question, I'm sure that the Trial Chamber and everybody else would appreciate that. The -- Mr. Krajisnik's -- you could observe, couldn't you, Mr. Bjelobrk, that Mr. Krajisnik's job and his responsibilities as the president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly were very onerous and demanding, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik was very conscientious and industrious in that job, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you say, that he was industrious. But I am not sure, given my experience of the work of the parliament, that the other qualification that you introduced in your assertion stands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's clarify or try to sweep away any misunderstanding. Mr. Bjelobrk, of course you have significant disagreements, political disagreements, with Mr. Krajisnik which covered the whole of this period. That's understood, isn't it, by you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. We were members of the parties that had different political programmes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I took it that you were on a road to make a point on what Mr. Krajisnik could have done or not, and we are now on a side road. Please proceed, and try to come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I agree with that last observation of -- of Your Honour's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Back on the main road, I hope, Mr. Bjelobrk. Apart from the political disagreements which are obvious, the -- would you say that the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly from after the multiparty elections through to the crisis which emerged at the October 1991 session was, in all the circumstances, a functioning and generally pretty well-functioning political organ?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me to assess the work of the parliament generally, which I'm not sure that is a very gratifying task. But I do believe, looking back at 1991, that the parliament had not really fulfilled its duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that because -- well, what was the result that you believe the parliament should have achieved by the end of 1991 that it didn't?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of that particular generation of the MPs was to solve the then-problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, and given that at the close of the -- of the year 1991 we had a war, I believe that they failed to fulfill their duties, and their duty was -- is precisely that, given that they were the highest representatives of the Bosnian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a fairly major dispute, wasn't there, about the reference of the question of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Council for National Equality?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was indeed a topic. But as far as I know, when we look at Europe and the United States of America, there the issue of independence is a very specific one, which means that a given community gains a certain status. This cannot, however, apply to Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 simply because it was a member of a community that was called Yugoslavia. This is, of course, a different problem, and that is something that lawyers are very familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that the independence of the United States of America wasn't achieved without a certain difficulty, do you, Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are we on the main road or on the side road?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, we're on the main road, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious, isn't it, Mr. Bjelobrk? Mr. Bjelobrk, there was -- whatever the rights or wrongs of people's positions on the constitutionality, illegality, and so on, there was a very serious issue involving very sharp disagreement among the parties, wasn't there, as to the constitutionalisation in relation to the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the need to refer that issue to the Council for National Equality?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three national political parties held different views, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that issue was very much at the heart of the crisis - and it was a crisis, wasn't it - that emerged at the session on the 14th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis lasted much longer. I suppose that just as I have, you have had the opportunity of seeing some of the documents that this Tribunal has. The culmination of the whole crisis was indeed in October 1991; however, it had been in existence and developing for the previous seven or eight months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, perhaps I -- I would rephrase my question. When I referred to the crisis that emerged at the session on the 14th of October, then in light of what you said, yes, I will rephrase that. That issue was very much at the heart of the crisis that came to a head on the 14th and 15th of October, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we invite the witness to answer that question, already two questions ago you raised two issues in your question about whether it was an issue. The first issue is the constitutionality of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the second issue was whether this matter should be referred to the Council for National Equality. I would like to have a clear picture of what, in your next questions, is the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour is quite right to - - to invite me to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the second of those that I'm concerned about, Mr. -- Mr. Bjelobrk, just to make it clear, and to the Trial Chamber. It's the need to refer that issue to the Council of National Equality in accordance with the Constitution that I'm talking about. So there -- although I made them sound as though they're two different issues here, that's what I'm talking about. So to -- to try and wrap all these points, then, into as simple a question as -- as I can, the -- the question of the -- the requirement to refer independence or sovereignty issues to the Council for National Equality was at the heart of the crisis that came to a head on the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of national equality was demonstrated in the public political life ever since the multiparty elections took place. And this October session was just one of such instances. The Council for National Equality did not have the competencies as are known in the world. These duties were equally exercised by the Presidency, by the parliament, and so on, but the three national parties agreed to form a body under such a title. And I would just wish to indicate that this is not the kind of a body that is otherwise known in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A constitutional body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are taking a position in the issue at that time. The question quite simply was whether at this October session, whether the question whether or not to refer this issue to the Council for National Equality was the issue that culminated at that time the conflict, or at least was at the heart of the disagreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this was the major topic in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whatever your point of view, Mr. Bjelobrk, and the dispute on that particular issue, would you agree that the situation which Mr. Krajisnik faced on the 14th and 15th of October in his capacity as speaker of the Assembly was -- the president of the Assembly was an extremely difficult situation to handle?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was very serious, and objectively speaking any speaker of the parliament would be -- would be very responsible in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very quick and very difficult judgements needed to be made by anybody in that position, in this case, Mr. Krajisnik. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from -- or that is, excluding the part of your question when you mentioned the expeditiousness, I would say that we were performing our duties, but we were not making headway at the pace that we should have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the -- the reference to expedition, Mr. Bjelobrk, to clarify: You don't suggest that it would have been possible, do you, for Mr. Krajisnik to have deferred the whole question of how to deal with the walk-outs and whether the Assembly session should continue, to have deferred it for a few days to think about it? That wasn't possible, was it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my earlier testimony here on the 10th of November, 2004, I was played an intercept, I believe of 12th August 1991 between Milosevic and Karadzic, and there you can see that this was a -- a very dominant issue that could not and need not have been resolved in a couple of days because the whole country had been dealing with the issue for several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, do you suggest that in the situation which arose on the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, Mr. Krajisnik could have realistically acted as if he had absolutely no affiliation whatever to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that he could have acted that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was -- and to deal with it in a nutshell, please, Mr. Bjelobrk, because we've been over it -- the continuation of the session on the 14th and 15th of October -- in fact, on the 15th and by the other parties was plainly regarded by the SDS as illegal and unconstitutional, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have referred - in your statement particularly, and I think in your oral evidence, as well - referred to that session. It was the 8th Assembly Session of the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament. And you particularly quote a -- a few lines from a speech given by Mr. Karadzic. What you say is, "People take it seriously. It's not good" -- I'm sorry, what you quote is, "People take it seriously. It's not good what you're doing. Is this the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway to hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through? Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people into possible extinction because Muslim people will not be able to defend themselves if it comes to war here." And that's the end of that particular quoted passage. And then you say, "I recall when Karadzic made this statement that I was extremely alarmed by these words. At other times I may have taken these words as rhetorical threats, but in the situation we were in, it was a clear message. This outburst brought something to light. It brought their thinking out into the open." Now, first of all, Mr. Bjelobrk, it -- it may be something we've covered before, but Mr. Karadzic was generally, throughout the whole period before and during the war, given to very strong language, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I am not an expert in linguistic issues, but I believe that in politics it doesn't really matter what sort of language you use but what sort of policies you create and implement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelobrk, this isn't a seminar on politics, please. I just asked you a question. It's right, isn't it -- you're a politician. Mr. Karadzic is generally -- that was his style, wasn't it? Very strong language.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that there exists a problem of style. When you go out in public and you address the public, it is not a matter of style; it is a matter of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to give up on that one and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I think the witness addressed the matter you raised. You said he used strong language. What the witness says, more or less, is it's not a matter of language or language only, but it's also a matter of underlying policy. That could mean that if you use strong language, that you are taking very strong policy lines or that you are more forcefully supporting your views than others would do. So therefore the witness has answered your question. And there's -- "giving up" seems to be a comment which is not, in my view, fair to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say straight away, Your Honour, Your Honour has exhorted me this morning, as always, and correctly, to make my questions clear and concise. I was going to come on and will come on to the question of policies as a separate matter so that when I ask a question which relates very specifically and very clearly to the use of language, then, Your Honour, I do suggest it's incumbent upon the witness with the Trial Chamber's encouragement to answer that question, and then when I ask a question about policy, to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And not to answer the policy questions which I haven't yet asked when I've confined my question very clearly and very specifically to the point about use of language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the witness in his answer has explained that they are not separable, as you suggest in your questions. And the witness is entitled to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honour, with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- because they are seperable issues, and I ask the questions, Your Honour, subject to Your Honour's guidance, and they are different issues. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that this outburst, as you describe it, by Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic "brought their thinking out into the open." By "they," do you mean the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. He's the president of the party, and he is the one who represents the policies of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic's way of expressing himself in this sort of language was very different from Mr. Krajisnik's, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say they had the same policies?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said yes. They had the same policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think perhaps you just spoke a little bit faintly, Mr. Bjelobrk. You say it brought their thinking out into the open, so whoever else's thinking that you're talking about there, can we take it that you are including both Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in -- in that thinking?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Look at the Sarajevo Oslobodjenje interview in January 1992, and you will see that there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we will, Mr. Bjelobrk, because we will come to that. The -- at this point, October 1991, you say it "brought their thinking out into the open." So what thinking had previously been suppressed or hidden which was brought out into the open by this outburst?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, two -- there are two keywords that you quoted: That the people had to defend themselves from someone, and that there was a risk of them getting extinct. So these are the two key issues. And when you speak publicly, then these are the sorts of categories that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I -- I want you to explain, please, very clearly what critical elements of SDS policy were brought to light by Dr. Karadzic's speech and had not previously been clear to you.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat. Two keywords in that address were irresponsible to say the least, and time will show that that is so, and that is that one, people needed to defend themselves against another people. That's one thing. And the second thing is that they could be extinct. When you have a political leader who is supposed to be advocating harmony in a society comes out with something like that, then it is very likely that you are going to get a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say, Mr. Bjelobrk, then, that what came to light by this outburst of Dr. Karadzic was a policy of the SDS to proceed to war?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there was an intention behind that to move to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a -- some sort of revelation to you as a result of that speech, was it, of something you had not previously feared?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that that is how I felt at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you say that Dr. Karadzic's outburst revealed an SDS policy to bring about the extinction of the Muslim people in -- in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the possibility that he foreshadowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not quite what I asked you, Mr. Bjelobrk, but I'll do the question a different way. Do you say that what was revealed to you, among anything else that was revealed by this outburst, was that Mr. Krajisnik was part of some group who had as a policy the extinction of the Muslim people of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from the SDS backed away from the statement that you just quoted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, when -- when did the serious concern that there might be a civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina first come into your head? I'll just clarify perhaps, if I may, but then repeat the question. I'm -- I'm not putting it to you, Mr. Bjelobrk, that you yourself had any such policy, so I just want to make it clear. When did the serious concern that somebody might lead matters on to a civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina first come into your head?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came into my head in the summer. The first thing that prompted me to think in this way was the unsuccessful split meeting of the six presidents of the former Yugoslav republics, people who want to be involved in politics and deal with serious political analysis. Even though the details were quite minor at the time, you could notice at the -- for the first time at the time minor possibilities for concern. In October, things had already escalated, and many people were not sleeping well by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, part of the basically basic background is this, isn't it: There had already been a war, mercifully a short one, in Slovenia, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. A simple audible answer is -- is useful, Mr. Bjelobrk. And there had been and was still a very bloody war in Croatia, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDS, including Dr. Karadzic, were, as at 14th/15th of October, were angry about the position adopted particularly by the SDA in relation to the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that they had a different position from that of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's clear, Mr. Bjelobrk, but you say they weren't -- Dr. Karadzic wasn't angry about the -- the SDA's stance as at 14th/15th October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I specified my answer because to me in politics it's irrelevant whether somebody is angry or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I've asked you before, please, not to concern yourself with irrelevance but to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, looking at the last few questions, the war in Slovenia is something that could not be reasonably disputed; ongoing war in Croatia, the same. I think that any further exploring whether the SDA was angry or did not like at all what happened is not really something -- of course, it's clear that there was more than just disagreement, which you would have on a daily basis. It was a very special situation. That's clear from all the evidence we heard until now. So whether "angry" is the right word or a strong disapproval or that they did not like it at all is not something that assists the Chamber at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Circumstances are relatively clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll save the argument for another day, Your Honour, and proceed with questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, a continued firm adherence by the SDA to independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried with it, as at October 1991, didn't it, a clear risk of civil war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That assertion stands only from -- when you look at it from the point of view of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, whatever point of view and whoever was responsible, isn't it correct that a continued firm adherence by the SDA to independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried with it, as at October 1991, a clear risk of civil war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only from the point of view of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you -- you say, do you, if the SDS had simply accepted independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then there wouldn't have been a civil war? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly that is what I wish to say, but partly I want to say that there was an alternative which existed to your idea of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is not a category which is standard in the rest of the world. The SDS only offered the following political alternative: If that is what you want, then you will have war on your hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, if correspondingly or conversely if the SDA had unequivocally given up the policy of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you agree it is most unlikely there would have been a civil war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you will be surprised, but probably we don't have time for that. Had the SDA behaved like that - and it did not behave the way you say - there would still have been a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got one more topic, but this is the area -- I just need to clear up with Mr. Karganovic where we are on pieces of paper and printing and so on, if I might be given just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm coming to is the -- is the article, which in fact the witness referred to a short time ago, the article in Oslobodjenje - near enough, I suppose - which is already in evidence at P404. Your Honour, I have a B/C/S copy for the witness. It's the extra English copies I don't have for the practical reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd put it on the ELMO. We find the English version of P404. Mr. Registrar, the B/C/S version can be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very grateful, Your Honour. That -- that seems a -- an excellent practical solution. Your Honour, I'm just inviting Mr. Karganovic to -- to help with just identifying the particular bits of some rather ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was just concerned, Your Honour, because the Serbian version doesn't seem to be in incredibly user-friendly form. I hope the witness -- but the witness is familiar with the -- the article. That's pretty clear from his statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you should have in front of you the copy or a copy of the article from Oslobodjenje dated 26 January 1992, which you specifically referred to in paragraph 55 of your statement. And you said that your reaction to this article, which is an interview or a report based on an interview with Mr. Krajisnik, your reaction was negative for a number of reasons, and then you list them. You say in your statement at 55.1 -- you say that "Mr. Krajisnik says it's impossible for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain" -- "unitarian" is the word in one -- in your statement, but -- "unitary if Yugoslavia disintegrates." Now, you've used the word there. What do you understand your own use of the word, then, "unitarian" or "unitary"?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpret it to mean that Mr. Krajisnik said that the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina could be placed in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as its external borders are concerned?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking about territorial integrity. There is the variant with borders and the territory. I don't know if there is any other possibility. We're talking about the change of borders or the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he talks, doesn't he, after that particular passage, which is about ten lines down in the English -- "It is impossible for Bosnia to remain unitary if Yugoslavia disintegrates." He says, "That is what it is inevitable that Bosnia be transformed as soon as possible, that it adjust to the current time and that the federal unit of Bosnia and Herzegovina become a legal subject - I deliberately use the word 'legal' - of three completely equal peoples." And the three peoples that he has in mind there are, of course, the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he goes on, doesn't he -- over the page in the English, it's about -- under the next passage, the formation -- the question is "The formation of the Republic of Serb people in BH has caused much criticism." And then in the answer to that, about halfway into that answer or a little bit further on, he says -- he talks about Republic of Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "We did not want to say this out loud because the Assembly of the Serb People feel that a certain demarcation of the three national communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina is inevitable. A Muslim, a Croat, and a Serb Bosnia will be formed as a result of the demarcation. However, in no case will one state be formed at the expense of another." Now, Mr. Bjelobrk, would you accept that -- that throughout this article Mr. -- or the interview on which it's based apparently -- Mr. Krajisnik is at pains to stress the legality and the equal treatment of the three peoples, in whatever solution emerges?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. The first problem in the logical understanding of that message is that Bosnia and Herzegovina is not comprised only of the criteria implying ethnic groups. We are talking -- it's a question of how to treat the Paris Convention on Human Rights. There are people who simplify things to such an extent that you have a series of human... There were politicians who so simplified the definition of "human rights" that they only took into account ethnic belongingness, but they then went on to interpret that as lines of demarcation between the different peoples. Any other question about whether if we had amongst those peoples somebody who was not part of that community would stop at that. So there you -- you would have different positions which were difficult to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, can we be clear. When you say that your reaction to this particular article was negative, are you saying that it also revealed to you important features of Mr. Krajisnik's thinking which had not previously been apparent to you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These characteristics were noticeable before, but here they were publicly established, even systematized, if I may say it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the early months of 1992, Mr. Krajisnik, among others, was actively involved in negotiations or discussions presided over by Mr. Cutilheiro, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those led to an agreement known as the Lisbon Agreement, dated the 18th of March, 1992. Well, whether or not you remember the precise date, Mr. Bjelobrk, you -- you recall that there was a Lisbon Agreement as a result of the Cutilheiro talks reached in March 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that agreement included as a very important element what Mr. Krajisnik refers to as "cantonisation". That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that same understanding that the messages in the text by Mr. Krajisnik and what was implemented based on the Cutilheiro talks was on the same qualitative line. I am even convinced by the conclusions of the European Union when the Cutilheiro talk groups were formed that there was a difference there, so I cannot really draw a line between what Mr. Krajisnik was saying and what was being discussed at the Cutilheiro talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say that there was a significant divergence between what Mr. Krajisnik was saying in public, in this interview, and what he was saying publicly in relation to the Cutilheiro talks?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the date of the realisation of the Lisbon Agreement yourself. This was a couple of months after this interview. So I don't see -- I cannot really answer this question. I don't see any logic there, simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did it not become, after the date of this interview, whatever your reaction, did it not become apparent to you over the succeeding weeks -- this interview or report was 26th of January. Did it not become apparent to you over the succeeding weeks that Mr. Krajisnik, among others, was actively involved in trying to achieve some peaceful solution to this whole problem?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a circle of politicians on the public scene who tried or showed that they were trying to find a peaceful solution, but there was a period amongst us when I was aware that there were weapons being brought in, rockets, and so on. This is the overall picture, not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just a particular detail in the arrangement of a certain or particular politician. It's very important to see the whole context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in 55.7 of your statement given to this Tribunal -- you say that "The division" -- you say that "He" - that's Mr. Krajisnik - "says there will be demarcation between ethnic communities, when I" -- that's you, Mr. Bjelobrk -- "When I read this, it was clear that he was talking about the national break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Just pausing there, Mr. Bjelobrk, that was -- that was your assessment and your political position that what was under discussion by Mr. Krajisnik here involves something that you regarded as the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not as a problem between two different political stances. Allow me to refer back to my profession. I am a nuclear energy expert by profession, so I understand a lot of things. When you have a social community in which citizens of different ethnic communities live, like the spots on a tiger's skin, completely mixed up, having a line of demarcation indicates that you want to transfer me or resettle me by force somewhere else. So that is basically the idea behind his words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you say that the idea behind Mr. Krajisnik's active participation and support for the -- for the Cutilheiro proposals was also designed to achieve the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question properly, I don't think that Mr. Cutilheiro was working towards that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you agree, Mr. Bjelobrk, that to the extent to which Mr. Krajisnik was supporting the Cutilheiro proposals, he was not working towards that either?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specify anything in terms of that for one simple reason: The idea of Mr. Krajisnik was based on lines of demarcation, and the idea of Mr. Cutilheiro implied cantonisation in the modern sense of that word, regionalization, the way it's done in Europe. And these two are completely different positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik refers expressly, doesn't he -- you've referred to the way it's done in Europe, and Mr. Krajisnik refers, doesn't he -- it's the - first, second, third, fourth, fifth heading -- "And does such a model exist in the world"? Do you see that heading? It's probably about halfway -- maybe about halfway through. Do you see that heading? And the reference immediately after that heading to "It exists in Belgium and in Switzerland."

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's clear, isn't it, that Mr. Krajisnik is appealing to some other European models as a basis for a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood your question properly. Is it clear that Mr. Krajisnik is drawing upon other models in Europe? Is that the right understanding of your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I've understood this text properly, of all the European experiences, Mr. Krajisnik is drawing upon the examples of multi-ethnic countries, and these are Belgium and Switzerland. In my experience, these would be the proper models to draw upon when thinking about such a concept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your party's position in relation to the Cutilheiro proposals as they came to -- towards the Lisbon Agreement in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite simple. First of all, all the principles of the Charter of Human Rights and the European Statute should be taken into account when developing such a concept, and one needs to be very open. However, in -- in this respect, all the national parties had views that were quite contrary to these -- these international provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- in very simple terms, would -- would you describe your party's position as for the Cutilheiro proposals, against, or for with reservations, against with reservations?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Politically speaking, I am absolutely against the Cutilheiro plan, but it was a good political move at the time because it served to calm down the political players.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. Mr. Krajisnik, would you have any questions to Mr. Bjelobrk, and could you give us an estimate on how much time you would need for that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have questions for Mr. Bjelobrk. I hope that I will be able to work on my notes now because I have to omit the questions already put to the witness by Mr. Stewart, and I will use the break to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's appreciated. We'll adjourn until 11.00. Time made available for the Defence was one-and a half hour. Approximately 1 hour and 20 minutes have been used. If you would need 15 or 20 minutes, the Chamber would not oppose. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. At the same time, I'll use the time to remind the parties that you're still to negotiate and attempt to reach a compromised solution on the B/C/S translation of a record of interview for Witness 648. And as far as I'm aware of, we have not heard yet from the parties whether such a compromise was reached. I don't expect an immediate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's Mr. Tieger's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know it's being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, the Chamber gives an opportunity to Mr. Krajisnik to put additional questions to you. Mr. Krajisnik, you may proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Krajisnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12 years later, I would first like to say hello to Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad to see you again and to see that you look well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to -- for the both of us actually to make a break in order for the interpreters to have time to interpret what we say. Mr. Bjelobrk, you will remember that last time a statement was mentioned of me having voted against on one item in June -- in July 1992 -- rather, 1991 for a proposal of yours. That was something that was proposed by your party. I will now refer to specific pages of the minutes from that particular session, and I would kindly ask for it to be placed on the ELMO. The first page - that's document 54 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have these documents? Do we have an English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you remember, Your Honours, those are the entire binders of the Assembly sessions that I had delivered to the Trial Chamber. I don't know if you have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know we also received a copy of those sessions shortly after Mr. Bjelobrk testified last time, but we just received B/C/S. We didn't translate them because we weren't intending to use them, and I don't know what portions we're talking about today. I don't know if there are any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were never tendered into evidence, were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber -- if you want to put something to a witness and use documents, then they should be provided in both languages. Do you have a copy of the document you would like to confront the witness with? Do you have a copy there? In whatever language? Yes. Do you have -- do you have a spare copy? Let me just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can have a look at it. These are the three pages that I would like to use. Your Honours, if I may put forward a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelobrk will read that part of the stenographic record, and then he can simply say whether at that time he was wrong about something or not, and that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that we'll put on the ELMO the relevant portion, that we invite the witness to read the relevant part, and if the witness can say anything about it, that there would then be translated subsequently and tendered into evidence. That is my suggestion at this moment. I see, Mr. Krajisnik, that you have given numbers. Is this your only copy, or do you have another copy? Could this be used for the witness? Yes. Well, CD-ROM is difficult to just read at this moment, unless you would give it to someone who could put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if this would happen again, would you please, to the extent that security issues do not oppose, provide the CD to the Chamber so that -- or to the registrar so that they could be printed out at this very moment. If you would please give them to the registrar at this moment, but we'll start first of all to proceed on the basis of these documents. They will then be used on the ELMO. And if you would just give guidance on what pages to be put on the ELMO. Yes? And at the same time, to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suggest the following: There's a CD-ROM. If the usher could open this CD, and if we could place it within the software, and then Mr. Bjelobrk could view them on the Sanction and they would be there, the documents, for all to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no problem with that if it's well prepared. We'll ask the registrar to open the CD, to see whether he could find the relevant pages. He would need the clues for that. And at the same time, this will be put on the ELMO so that the witness can be confronted with it. May I take it -- you said three pages, Mr. Krajisnik. I see that you've got four pages here. We'll deal with them in the order as you provided them, Mr. Krajisnik. I see that there are some blue markings. I take it that these are the portions you want to draw the attention of the witness to. And you can look at the screen, as well, to see what we have. Could you please give them to the usher, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. But this is my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you have all the -- these documents on the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Krajisnik, we're not prepared at this moment for opening -- please give them whatever is on the document. You'll see that on your screen once the usher has put them on the ELMO. Just prepare them in the right order and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, page 54. That's the continuation of the session of the Assembly and the chamber on the 27th of June, 1991. Mr. Bjelobrk can read the highlighted part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please slowly read it so that the interpreters can follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Krajisnik speaking: "Gentlemen, we are resuming the session of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I owe you an explanation. At the yesterday's session, the SDP deputies announced and acted upon their announcement, which was that a group of the deputies walked out on the session. Under the rules of procedure, under such circumstances we need to make a one-hour interval. I owe you an explanation as to why we did not grant that one-hour break which otherwise is provided by the rules of procedure. "Upon the adoption of the agenda, I gave the floor to Mr. Izetbegovic. Mr. Izetbegovic was supposed to make a short intervention, which he did later on. "Mr. Lazovic asked to be given an opportunity to reply, and in some way thus interrupted the announced intervention by Mr. Izetbegovic." That's the end of the first document. The next document: The president of the deputies' club, Mr. Miro Lazovic, is the one addressing the Assembly here. This was in the aftermath of some debates. "We accept all the suggestions and comments given by the legislative legal commission in relation to the text of this resolution. They are first and foremost of a law-related nature, so to speak. They do not change the gist of the resolution, and we also accept the title proposed by the legislative and legal commission. In essence, it doesn't mean anything, but it, rather, explains contents of the text, that this is above all a document expressing political will." And I would seize this opportunity - I don't know if there is any need to read it - to put forward this to you. The third document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just for my information, are you just reading what it reads, including the last lines? Is that what the document says? Where you said, "In essence, it doesn't mean anything, but it, rather, explains it is contents of the text, that this is above all a document" -- and that's literally all the text we find here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- these are the words of Irfan Ajanovic, a member of the SDA, therefore, from the Muslim side. I quote: "From this rostrum, I would issue a mild protest to the SDA deputies for their behaviour and conduct in relation to the SDP deputies at the yesterday's session. They were unable to honour what was said by the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was given the floor by the president of the Assembly. He almost reached the rostrum and wanted to address us, and while the president was discussing a very important matter, the auditorium was also in the position to listen and to see. The SDP deputies walked out from this chamber. I believe that I share the opportunity -- or, rather, I believe that the SDA deputies share the opinion of a large number of deputies in this Assembly and that should not -- it should not have been done in the form of a protest." And now we will go on to the address by Miro Lazovic. Miro Lazovic is the head of the deputies' club of Mr. Bjelobrk's party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may put a text to the witness. You are not supposed to explain who is who because then you are providing the information where the witness is supposed to do so. So you are now quoting the words of Mr. Lazovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I simply did not have the opportunity of consulting our deputies. As far as I've managed to exchange opinions with my peers to overcome this position, we believe that the Assembly should speak its mind on the conclusions of the Assembly and that it should be done in the way proposed by the legislative legal commission." Momcilo Krajisnik: "I have to put to vote this conclusion that was now amended by the proposing party and by the legislative legal commission. First, we should vote on the conclusion. I am putting to vote the conclusion put forth by the proposing party based on the intervention Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the legislative legal commission. Who is in favour? Who is against? Five are against. Those abstaining: Three abstained votes. I voted in favour; 121 voted for. An applause. "Please, we are putting to vote this statement. Can we all vote? Who is in favour of the statement?" This is the statement put forth by the SDP. I'm continuing my quote: "The amendments that were provided by them are in order, I believe. Who is in favour? 121. Who is against? Six. Who abstains? I abstain myself, in fact. "Gentlemen, I thank you for making it possible for me not to walk out of the parliament. I thank you for voting unanimously for this because we are trying to produce a statement of the political will in favour of calming down the people. In ten days this will be a platform that we will be able to work on. We stand adjourned for the day," and the session closed at 14.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you did not only read but you also explained what statement or what proposal was put to the vote. You're not supposed to add anything to it. If you would like to have this clarified, you should ask the witness. Would you please now put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you've seen the stenographic record from that session.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the contribution of Mr. Krajisnik was to have this proposal voted.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my understanding of the text that you quoted: We offered a document that was aspiring towards proposing a definite solution. The debate that preceded the vote made it quite unlikely that the document would be discussed at all because you see that in the first instance the discussion focussed on the conclusion rather than the SDP proposal. I wish to remind you that this is already the time when the SDS deputies had walked out. When you offered the document to vote, it got 121 votes in favour and you abstained. And I'm talking now about the proposal and not about the conclusion of the legislative legal commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make this quite clear to the Trial Chamber, would the conclusion have been voted -- passed had Mr. Krajisnik not voted in favour?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you're talking about the conclusion, you did support it with your vote but not the proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would your document have been put to vote at all had the conclusions not been voted?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they would not have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- would your platform have 121 votes without Mr. Krajisnik's vote having been known previously?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please make a pause between question and answer. I'm just trying to understand what you said, Mr. Bjelobrk. Do you say that it was not your proposal that was voted upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November, I tried to explain the overall situation. First of all, it was controversial whether our document would be out for debate at all. The findings of the legislative legal commission with this conclusion by Mr. Lazovic was of a legal and procedural nature. The participation of Mr. Krajisnik was that by participating he made this possible because in the meantime the SDS deputies had left the Assembly session. That is why he created the conditions for proper procedure, and this is quite proper. But when we came to the realisation of the things that were supposed to contribute to a calming-down of the situation, we got to these results when Mr. Krajisnik abstained. In November I tried to explain this problem of responsibility where you as the president of the Assembly stay, you create technical conditions for work, but basically it's a question of obstruction because we all know that this platform was never again actually adopted by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the last session, you objected and you said that the SDS and Krajisnik were in favour of the division of Sarajevo. I would now like to ask the girl ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you assist Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, would you like to have these documents you just have in evidence? The documents you just showed to the witness. I think it would be proper to have them in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you provide copies as soon as possible without any markings on it, and then they'll have to be translated before a final decision can be taken as to whether or not to admit them into evidence. So the original will be given back to you -- no, we'll keep it for a while. You have to -- so that we can see that we received the same. Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is one of the maps from the Vance-Owen Plan -- actually, from the book by Mr. Owen. Do you see there that a division of Sarajevo is planned?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the map of the contact group from 1994, and division of Sarajevo is not planned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see in the -- the last figure on the one side and the other side where you have the federation and the Serb entity?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not see the figures and did not catch the answer by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to make a pause between question and answer since the answer of the witness was not heard. Apart from the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that I can read even on my screen that for the Federation it's 51 per cent and for the Serb entity it is 49 per cent. Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone can read that. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik, and take care that you make a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to read the figure before last in the Federation, in the sum for the Serbian entity.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one before last for the Federation is 1.31 per cent, and the one for the Federation is 8.25 per cent. These are the numbers, one but last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, in the Federation column, do you see 2.07 per cent?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the last figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see 1.04 under the Serb entity column?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please scroll the page up a little bit. Very well. I'm sorry, could you please scroll it up. On the map, where you see "Sarajevo," do you see the number 3.11 per cent?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you add up these figures, whether it -- it really does come to 3.11 per cent.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
