utterances.text: Now, I -- it's totally unclear to me what figures have been added by the witness. What now is added to reach the sum of 3.11 per cent? Is that the 2.07 from the Federation, last on the list of numbers before a sum is reached, and the Serb entity 1.04? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are now adding numbers from the one list to a number from the other list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please scroll up. Thank you. Could you please scroll down. A little bit more, please. Could we look at the map on the left, please, and scroll down a little bit. I really apologise. I would like to look at the map because you can't see it very well on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please zoom out a tiny little bit and move a bit higher so that the map is on the screen. Yes. There we are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if we can see the whole map, please. Maybe we can move to the next document. I cannot find here what I am looking for. The next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on this map that -- a ratio 2 to 1 division of Sarajevo is planned, on the bottom of the map?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the text which says, "Sarajevo district, 3.1 per cent." I don't see any other indications about all -- the only thing is in the third and the fourth lines -- no, no, I don't see any other elements for definition of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the following text, please: "The total for the majority Muslim republic, including the area of Sarajevo, on the basis of 2:1."

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on the map that it says in the Sarajevo district 3.1 per cent?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, please. This document you can take away. That's a map of Sarajevo. I think that there are several copies there, so could you please give me a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I'm reluctant to intervene, but we do have time constraints in the amount of time we have to present our case, and I'm not sure what the point is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding these 1993, 1994 maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. I'll say a few things about it soon. Mr. Krajisnik, what's your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you have a document in front of you that was in Dayton at the start of the negotiations, and that document mentions the district. I would just like to ask you whether you are familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I don't know the document. I don't know who drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a document from Dayton.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But who is the author? There were several authors. This is the position of the contact group, such as the maps that we saw or of somebody else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you know this document. Were you in the process of it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the witness had already answered the question that he did not know the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to read the first paragraph of this document in Serbian. Perhaps you can read the whole document which was in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What are you, then -- since the witness doesn't know the document, Mr. Krajisnik, what did you have in mind to ask him? Because if it's just reaching conclusions on the basis of a text, there's no need to ask the witness about it since the Chamber can read the text, as well, and one might try to find a way of introducing this document ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness in front of him has a document which during Cutilheiro's time, and it was also presented during the Dayton Agreements. That's why I asked him if he knew about, but if he doesn't know, very well. In that case, I would like him to return the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions to the witness, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [I0nterpretation] Yes. Yes, I have more questions. I will try to be more expedient now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the heading of this document and tell us what date it's from?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date is the 17th of January, 1992, and the -- I know. I can see the title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the title, please. The subheading, please.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cite Dr. Radovan Karadzic. "The rest of Yugoslavia must be consolidated." Dr. Biljana Plavsic: "We looked at the backs of those who destroyed Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, just one moment, please. I am going to read it, and you can confirm it. "Press conference of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia- Herzegovina in Sarajevo." The large heading: "Not division but transformation of Bosnia." I would now like you to scroll the text down. In the bottom left corner, it says, "Namely, with a realistic transformation of Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina will have to transform itself, and nobody should be trying to say that this is a division of this republic. This is a transformation whereby the sovereignty of all three constitutive peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina are -- their position is being made stronger." Is that what it says, Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's entirely unclear to us -- it has not been introduced whose words they are, who did write them down. It seems to be a press conference. But whether these were your words or the words of Mr. Vance or Mr. Owen or Mr. Karadzic is totally unclear to us. But -- therefore it does not really assist the Chamber to introduce these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like the document to be placed on the ELMO again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the words of Mr. Karadzic? Could you please look.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a quote mark at the beginning for someone. Yes. After the first subheading, his name is mentioned and that this is what he says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least, the newspaper says that these are the words of Mr. Karadzic, which is, of course, not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my point, Your Honour. If he wants to submit these newspaper articles, we don't need Mr. Bjelobrk to sit in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. courtroom and take up our time translating if he has no specific comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I already hinted at such a solution, that if you want to introduce these kind of documents, where the witness could hardly say anything about it or hardly add anything to it -- there are other ways of doing that, Mr. Krajisnik. Do you have any question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to be as brief as possible. You will remember that Mr. Bjelobrk claimed that he thought that the Serbian Democratic Party wanted a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We're talking about the 17th of January here, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, so then the question would be for the witness to confront him with this publication and ask him whether on the basis of this publication he still sticks to the answer he's given or whether that changes his mind. That's what you, then, should ask him because the mere fact that a newspaper publishes something which is not consistent with the witness's answer doesn't necessarily mean that the newspaper is right and the answer of the witness is wrong. Mr. Krajisnik, you're limiting your time. I said I would not mind if you would take a little bit more than granted to the Defence. I'll grant you another five minutes, and then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could the usher please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regionalisation was discussed and that it's impossible to regionalise Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is an extract of the assembly meeting of the 25th and 26th of January, 1992. Could you please read the words of Mr. Muhamed Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, is this the BiH Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the last Assembly session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please point to what part you'd like to witness to read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text where Muhamed Cengic is speaking. Mr. Bjelobrk has that in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to inform you about something and suggest something. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina received instructions and adopted a decision to carry out regionalisation, a new regionalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that the Serbian Democratic Party, as well as the Party of Democratic Action and the Croatian Democratic Union should provide their proposals on the type of regionalisation, what kind of regionalisation it should be. What should be done? I think it should be useful for us to carry out this regionalisation. This is a task given by the government, that we schedule a referendum, determine deadlines for the referendum and a deadline for that regionalisation. There will be no referendum before we receive a complete plan for the regionalisation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Next document, please. Just one question: What was the function of Mr. Muhamed Cengic in the government and in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Prime Minister of the Executive Council of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also the vice-president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read on what Mr. Cengic says.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sir, Doctor, this is how we agreed, and let us then conclude that here together before everybody."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when Mr. Cengic and Mr. Karadzic were together in front of the microphone?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does Muhamed Cengic say?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Please accept that the referendum be held on the 10th instead of on the 1st of March. Alija Izetbegovic, if you are interested, Mr. Kreso."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please. Next document, please. Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it doesn't make much sense to show us documents on the ELMO and then to say that now the next document may be shown. You can ask the witness questions but nothing else. Apart from that, your time is on. I suggest to you that you discuss with counsel about a practical way of introducing documents you consider relevant for your defence and to find a way -- how to introduce them. You may have noticed that sometimes contextual documents or -- that's about municipalities, but I can imagine that even contextual documents on Assembly sessions could be produced. Of course, if there's any contradiction between those already in evidence and those produced in this way, then we should find a way to settle that and give the parties an opportunity to argue on what's the best document reflecting what happened during certain meetings, and then the Chamber will finally decide upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just make a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- an inquiry. When Your Honour suggests to Mr. Krajisnik that he discusses with counsel a practical way of introducing documents, does Your Honour mean with Defence counsel, prosecuting counsel, or both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggested to him to discuss it with Defence counsel, and, of course, if there would be any need to consult with Prosecution counsel in order to find a way to introduce those documents, of course, that would be the logical thing to do at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just had in mind that it's really as much an issue between prosecuting counsel and Mr. Krajisnik as between Mr. Krajisnik and Defence counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think my suggestions were clear until now, and I do understand that you'd rather have Mr. Krajisnik to deal directly with the Prosecution. At least, that's how I understood it. That's not part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't go quite that far, Your Honour. But I was indicating -- well, some of the underlying practical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- considerations in this rather unusual system that we have at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's good that you didn't go that far, because it was not part of my suggestion either. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would just like to ask you to allow me one question regarding what I showed to Mr. Bjelobrk and then one more question in relation to Sarajevo, and then I will finish my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you will remember this session. I would ask you whether Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew this proposal by Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that, but I think that Cengic's option did not pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just this one document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and this document, as well. They go together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll recall that when we were talking about Serbs leaving Sarajevo. Were you aware that there was a decision by the city Assembly that Serbs can leave or that they can stay?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I followed the atmosphere very specifically, and I knew about that decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you place the next document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we first identify what documents we're talking about. Is this Oslobodjenje, or does it just look like that? And could we also have a look at the date. Is it somewhere in 1995 or is that ...? It looks very much as mid-February 1996, even. Is that correct, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a decision of the city Assembly that Serbs can leave Sarajevo. Another document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The city Assembly of Sarajevo, I do understand. What part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian Sarajevo. At that time it was Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed about the threats expressed by the Federation in relation to the Serbs who were supposed to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were threats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But since I am out of time, I will stop now though, even though I do have a lot more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, any need to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no questions for the witness either. Then there's no question about whether questions in redirect or questions from the Bench have triggered any need to re-examine the witness. Mr. Bjelobrk --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understood, although I'm not asking you to take advantage of it -- I had understood - but perhaps my memory is playing tricks, which does happen -- that I might have an opportunity of asking questions after Mr. Krajisnik. But on this occasion, Your Honour, I'm not needing to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good that you remind me, that due to the sensitive elements in the relation between the questions put by Defence counsel and by the accused that there might be a need. But there's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. I'm grateful for that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelobrk, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much, not for coming once only, but even for coming two times. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the Chamber would like to have an early break. That means that we'd have a break now for 20 minutes, and then after the break we would resume the cross-examination of Mr. Prstojevic. If we have a break now, then there would be a time remaining, approximately one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to raise the issue of exhibits with Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather, especially since it's a bit unclear what to do with the exhibits that Mr. Krajisnik might tender, I wonder whether all of them are -- the problem is also that they were given back to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, everything you've shown to the witness was on the ELMO. To that extent, it is on the record. They also have all been read. You are invited to the extent you think that they would have to be in evidence to provide clean copies so that translations can be prepared and that we can decide on the admission into evidence. And, of course, after the translation is there, then the Prosecution could make any objections it would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They're Exhibits 392 to 406, for purposes of -- of the record that we want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- seek admission of later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's deal with the exhibits at a later stage. But we'll not forget it. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to say a few things to you in respect of your examination of witnesses. First of all, I'd like to clearly express that what you did, for example, with the previous witness, clarifying that a photograph where certain people appear was a photograph taken in a reception certainly adds to creating a context which enables the Chamber to better understand the evidence as it was there. On the other hand, the way you dealt with the documents today did not assist the Chamber in any way, and I think that it would be wise to seek further guidance and further information from your counsel, how to deal with these kind of matters, and you could even wonder whether it would not be wiser to leave handling documents in the hands of counsel. The Chamber allowed you today more time than was envisaged to do it. The Chamber is not willing to spend more time on inadequate handling of documents in the examination of a witness. Then we will proceed with the cross-examination of the next witness, the witness that was still waiting, Mr. Prstojevic. Mr. Or Madam Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, just using the time, may I say, Your Honour, in relation to the apparently entirely unresolved question of how the guideline 60 per cent applies in this situation, I don't -- a number of comments to be made. I've said nothing. I don't wish to be taken to have accepted anything in relation to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My position is entirely reserved as far as what I might say in relation to that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber is neither seeking to spend more time on cross-examination as of now. At the same time, the Chamber is also not seeking a new source for a conflict between you and Mr. Krajisnik. So we'll have to deal with that at a later stage, and we'll have to reconcile these two elements. Mr. Stewart, you may continue your cross-examination of Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before doing so, Mr. Prstojevic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And for your information, Mr. Stewart, in the beginning of the cross-examination, quite some time was spent on clarifying issues which are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ambiguities in statements which are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I -- well, I understand that, Your Honour. I don't quite understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In fact, there was quite some time spent on unprecise or unclear information. At least, that's how we understood it. It's just that if you say no, I was doing something else, then we have to re-read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I was doing that, Your Honour, but I was doing it legitimately because the fact that something is not in evidence does not mean that it may not be a fact which in cross-examination with the witness I nevertheless wish to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully agree with you if you think that those portions -- well, the transcripts that are not in evidence, that they nevertheless give rise to eliciting evidence from a witness and then in a clear fashion, rather than in an unclear way, as you may have found it in the transcript. That's, of course -- you're fully entitled to that if you find it of such importance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you talked about -- you were asked about -- certain questions about the -- the structure of the Serb Democratic Party, and in your earlier oral evidence this week we went over a certain amount of familiar territory there. So far as the Main Board of the SDS is concerned, can you say from your recollection how often that body met in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How frequently the Main Board met in 1991 is not something I know because I was not a member of the Main Board. As for 1992, from April onwards the party was non-active, I believe, until the end of the year, until the Jahorina plenary when the party would resume its operation, both the Main and the Executive Boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are able, whether or not you were present yourself -- but does that mean that you are able to give some figures or some assessment of how many times the Main Board ever met in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot because I do not know how many times it met until the April 1992, and I believe the Jahorina plenary was held at the end of the year; although, I am not certain about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence earlier in this case - this is at page 64. Your Honour, I'm talking about the -- the transcript numbered obviously from 1 to whatever for Tuesday of this week, rather than the continuously numbered transcript. So it's at page 64, lines 10, 11 - you said, "In terms of hierarchy, the work of the Municipal Boards was orchestrated by the Main Board." First of all, when you said "the work of the Municipal Boards," can we take it that you -- you actually only really have any worthwhile knowledge about the activities or the work of your own municipality board, rather than that of -- those of other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the operation of our Municipal Board. I believe that the communication flow and the coordination of work was the same for all the Municipal Boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's just an assumption you make, Mr. Prstojevic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the latter part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So talking about your own Municipal Board, that work, you say, was orchestrated by the Main Board. Well, first of all, you've clearly given evidence that in the hierarchy of the SDS, the Main Board came above the municipality board. But in what -- when you say "orchestrated," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Republican Assembly of the Serb Democratic Party, the Main Board is the highest body. The Main Board comprises the Executive Board as its executive body, in fact. All the documents, statements, position papers, or decisions were sent from the Main Board to the Municipal Board or from the Executive Board to the Municipal Board. However, in Sarajevo we had the city board of the Serbian Democratic Party for Sarajevo, which sometimes emerged as a structure in between, which had its own meetings, and the materials produced by this board were sent directly to the Municipal Board, which had to familiarise itself with the document and implement it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, was there a clear hierarchy among the Main Board of the SDS, the Executive Board of the SDS, the city board of Sarajevo, and the Ilidza municipality board?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly there was a hierarchy in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Prstojevic, my question was something not -- it wasn't whether there clearly was a hierarchy but whether the hierarchy was clear. Let me make it more specific. It seems a possibility - say whether this is right from the answers that you've given - that there was a less than clear hierarchy and interrelationship between, number one, the neighbourhood and Executive Board of the SDS; number two, the city board of Sarajevo; and number three, the Ilidza municipality board. Do you -- do you agree that there was a less-than-clear hierarchy and interrelationship among those?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I disagree. The hierarchy of the party was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Was the city board in any way in between the Main Board and the Executive Board and the Ilidza municipality board?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sometimes the Main Board would receive materials direct from the Main Board or the Executive Board and sometimes receive materials via the city board of Sarajevo. Is that or is that not the position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- yeah, I think if Mr. Stewart looks at the question, he'll see it's -- it's unclear. It's the Main Board receiving materials from the Main Board. I'm sure that's not what he intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I -- you're absolutely right. I didn't. Slip of the tongue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes the Ilidza municipality board - thank you for that - sometimes the Ilidza municipality board would receive materials direct from the Main Board or the Executive Board of the SDS, and sometimes it would receive materials from those bodies via the city board of Sarajevo. Is -- is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to return though to press you, Mr. Prstojevic, on what you meant by saying, "The work of the Municipal Board of Ilidza was orchestrated by the Main Board." Do you mean any more than receipt of whatever correspondence or other documents came through one route or another from the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that there was written correspondence and telephone communication on a daily basis and that, where necessary, there were also personal contacts with the members of both the Main and Executive Boards. In addition to that, members of the Main Board and people's deputies were also in charge of dealing with Municipal Boards. They were duty-bound to take part in the work of the Municipal Board of Ilidza, to follow the board's work, assist, and ultimately to evaluate its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally ever on the receiving end of telephone calls made on behalf of the Main Board in relation to the activities of your Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the Municipal Board full-time. I did not have a desk there. But we had a secretary of the board and a technical secretary who worked there full-time. At the end of my working hours at my workplace, I would drop by the board's premises and try to keep abreast of the communications, the mail that arrived. There were cases when President Karadzic called me over the phone, and, of course, there were cases when I placed a phone call to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The secretary of your Municipal Board was Mr. Momcilo Ceklic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The secretary of our Municipal Board during my term of office was Ignjat Simic, and I cannot recall the lady's -- or, rather, the name of the lady who was the technical secretary. I believe her name was Biljana. Momo Ceklic is the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Ilidza. He was a functionary in the multiparty Assembly established in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how often during the period from when you were first elected in June 1991 through -- let us take it to April 1992. How often did you or the people working for you -- did the Municipal Board receive a call from Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic did not call very often, because there was the Executive Board and the people who -- there were the people who were on duty in the Executive and the Municipal Boards. In fact, I can only remember one phone call placed by Dr. Karadzic, and I know that I called him two or three times, asking him to receive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in relation to the issue about replacement of a secretary?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, was what in relation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That contact, that phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I only say that because the witness indicated there was one phone call placed by Dr. Karadzic and two or three phone calls by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, you're quite right. I -- I'd probably jumped to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all those phone calls to do with an issue relating to the replacement of a secretary?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had quite a long conversation with our president in relation to the dismissal of a secretary in Kasindol. There was just this one conversation where I was told that -- that everything was proceeding in accordance with the procedure and the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is -- is the answer that those phone calls that you described, those very few phone calls between you and Dr. Karadzic, did all at least include the issue of the replacement of dismissal of that local secretary in Kasindol?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was exactly the issue we discussed, only about the removal of the secretary because the local board there wanted to proceed in a way that was contrary to the procedure in place and hastily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of anybody -- let's leave aside Dr. Karadzic without exploring that. But can you recall the names of anybody who telephoned to the Municipal Board in Ilidza between end of June 1991 and April 1992 on behalf of either the Main Board or the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something I really cannot remember. There was Mr. Velibor Ostojic from Ilidza, who was a member of the Main Board. We also had the people's deputy, Ljubo Bosankic, who was a deputy representing Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. This facilitated our communication to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. You may have noticed I'm looking for a piece of paper, which is just hard to find while I'm proceeding. I wonder if I might just take two minutes to see -- or less to if I can see if I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Less than two minutes. It was driving me nuts, and probably everybody else looking at my trying to find it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Prstojevic, according to information which comes from a report which you will have been spared but which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is Mr. Treanor's report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are only six meetings of the Main Board of the SDS recorded to have occurred between October 1991 and April 1992. We have the dates, but I won't trouble you, unless anybody presses me to, with all the detailed dates. But there was one in November, two in December of 1991, one in February 1992 and two in March of 1992. So that's six meetings in five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just excuse me, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt. And I -- I think it's fair to note that if it's Mr. Treanor's report we're -- that Mr. Stewart is relying on, that was based, as he told us, on the documentation available to the OTP, not necessarily an exhaustive -- or reflection of all the meetings that might have been recorded and are reflected elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Stewart, that you wanted to confront the witness with the information on the basis of minutes available that during that period, we are aware at this moment, of a certain number of meetings. Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Mr. Tieger's point is a perfectly fair one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had attempted to cover it by the use of the word "recorded." Of course, Mr. Tieger could say it might have been recorded in a lot of different ways. So, yes, I should make it clear. On the basis of what we see, or Mr. Treanor's evidence, what have been identified by him as recorded, there were those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, would you have any information that would enable you to confirm or reject or qualify the suggestion that there were of the order of six meetings of the Main Board during that period November 1991 to March 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information whatsoever on the basis of which I could confirm either way, and I cannot speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I say to you -- and it's a bit more specific -- that between July 1991 and the 26th of February -- end of July, 1991 and the 26th of February, 1992, the same report, same sources, we have nine sessions of the Executive Board. In that case, they are, I believe, identified as first and ninth sessions. Do you -- again, do you have any knowledge which enables you to confirm, deny, qualify the proposition that there were of the order of nine Executive Board session during that period?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it earlier on, that in this period I attended only one Assembly session, and that was the Republican Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party. However, it does seem logical that the Main Board -- that the Executive Board should have met more frequently than the Main Board. I believe that is something that applies everywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have -- did you have more contact yourself or through your secretaries of the Main Board with the Executive Board than with the Main Board, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had more contacts with the Executive Board because the Executive Board is a direct operational body which works with -- directly with the Municipal Boards to implement the policies planned. Whatever was agreed or decided upon had to be then discussed on a daily basis in order to ensure the implementation of the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember who it -- who on behalf of the Executive Board you dealt with during that period, June/July 1991 through to April 1992? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the first president of the Executive Board was Mr. Velibor Ostojic. There was Rajko Dukic after him. But most of the contacts we had were with the secretary of the Executive Board, and that was Mr. Trivko Komad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, just concentrating for the moment, Mr. Prstojevic, on who you dealt with, rather than who held offices, you've said that most contacts were with Mr. Komad, was it? How often -- let's stick all along with the period from end of June 1991 to April 1992 for the -- for the moment. During that period, how often were you personally in direct contact with Mr. Komad?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contact with him on several occasions, as many times as I needed to, but I cannot remember, not even approximately, how many times that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you couldn't tell us, then, for -- you say you couldn't remember even approximately. Do you mean that you couldn't even tell the Trial Chamber whether it was six times or sixty times?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm trying to say. I could even call Mr. Trivko Komad five times in a day if I needed something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that something that happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably did. I think that it did. If I spoke with him or if I received some information about something that I had to do or to check, then I would get back to him. Or if I was asking for something, then I would be on that until it was finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep any sort of logbook or notebook of calls and activities on behalf of the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretaries of the Municipal Board and the protocol officer, the administrative person, would be the ones who would note down the calls in order to transfer them. I personally did not jot down the calls, and I don't have any kind of agenda or diary with notes on the party work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- so, Mr. Prstojevic, if you were, for example, as you suggest was a possibility, if you were talking to -- sorry. I've just forgotten the name for a moment. Mr. Trivko Komad. If you were talking to -- to him five times in a day, do you -- you say you didn't make any notes, then, of any of those calls or during those calls?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your practice in relation to calls to that gentleman was very different from the practice you are adopting in this courtroom, of keeping a fairly careful notebook of the questions that I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our practice that telephone calls with representatives of the Main Board, the Executive Board were not to be jotted down anywhere or recorded anywhere because we simply didn't need that. The only thing to be noted down was that if -- if I needed some information or some name, something that I couldn't remember, then I would do that as a reminder. What notes I'm making here, I didn't spend a minute thinking about my testimony here because my activities at home do not allow me or permit me to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Mr. -- I'm not quite sure whether the name is the right way around. But Mr. Trivko. We know who we're talking about. If Mr. Trivko indicated to you some action that was required on your behalf or on behalf of the Ilidza municipality board, you still wouldn't make any note of that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was simply not following you. I'm sorry, I wasn't concentrating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alright. No problem, Mr. Prstojevic. I'll repeat the question. If Mr. Trivko indicated to you on the telephone some action that was required on your behalf or on behalf of the Ilidza municipality board, you still wouldn't make a written note of that action. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I would not because that was how we worked, usually. It was easy to remember those tasks at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they weren't all that frequent? Such actions to be taken?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It had nothing to do with the frequency of the events. It was just the manner and the method of work in the SDS -- in the Ilidza SDS Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your secretaries follow the same practice as you of not needing to write down any such actions that were to be taken?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that the secretary and the technical secretary and the administrative staff member were obliged to note down calls, messages, everything else that had to be passed on or conveyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we just have the names, please. You've given us the name of the secretary. What was the name of the technical secretary?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ignjat Simic was secretary. The technical secretary was a woman; she was a lawyer. Her name was Biljana. We also had an administrative assistant. I don't remember her name; I know that she was from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any part of her name?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's important, that woman is now working in the Kasindol Hospital. I think her name is Mila. When I really strain or try very hard, then it comes to me. Perhaps later the last name also will come to me. She's working as a nurse in the Kasindol Hospital now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prstojevic. If the name does come back to you while you're giving evidence here, I'd be grateful if you could just then give it to the Trial Chamber and to me. Thank you. The -- in your evidence in this case at page 65, this was on Tuesday this week, you said that "Very often presidents of Municipal and city boards would be present at the Main Board meetings of the SDS." Was it that -- you say "very often." Was the position this: That in the fairly normal way, if you -- if people were available to go to such meetings and could with reasonable convenience go, then they would go? If they couldn't go for some reason, then it was perfectly acceptable to send apologies and not be there? Was -- was that the position?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but if it was like that, then that would be complete anarchy. We were obliged to attend the meetings if we were invited. If we were not invited, perhaps it was possible that somebody because for some need would attend uninvited, but they would have to request permission to attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prstojevic, in your own case, for example, whatever other meetings there might or might not have been, as I put before you earlier, between 21st November 1991 and 23rd of -- of March 1992, there were six, according to Mr. Treanor's report, clearly recorded Main Board meetings of the SDS, and yet during that period - and we'll come to that - but the maximum number of meetings you appear possibly to have attended during that time was one. That's right, isn't it? You -- you -- whether or not you even attended one, you didn't attend more than one meeting of the Main Board between November 1991 and March 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was there in 1991; that was in November. And then later I was at the Jahorina plenary meeting when the party was just starting its work. I did not attend other meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The Jahorina one you're talking about was way back before November 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jahorina plenary was in 1992 during the war, when the party was beginning its work. It was towards the end of the year. I believe that you have the date, probably, when this was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I -- I see myself and just ought to clear this up, then. In your previous answer when you talked about the Jahorina plenary meeting when the party was just starting its work. Confirm this, which appears from your answer. You mean starting its work during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's true. When it relaunched its work or renewed its work in the wartime period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had attended a meeting not in Jahorina, of course, but you had attended a meeting earlier in June 1991, hadn't you? Around the time that you took -- first took office.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know where that information comes from. I did not attend any meetings of the Main Board or the Assembly of the SDS in June, but I did at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those meetings that -- I've just reminded you of, those six recorded meetings. So the majority of those that you didn't attend, you -- did you send your apologies, or was that your practice to send your apologies if you couldn't attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't invited to these meetings, so I wasn't supposed to inform them about not attending, either. In order to clarify, I would like to say that the presidents of the Municipal Boards were not automatically members of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where you say in -- at page 65 on Tuesday this week, "and very often presidents of municipal and city boards would be present at the Main Board meetings, and so they would have heard all that," that's subject to the clarification you've just given that they were not automatic attenders. That's what you're saying, are you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I want to say, that they were not automatically obliged to come, nor was it made possible for them to attend automatically. Once the party renewed its work in the war, the presidents of the Municipal Boards would then attend the meetings of the Main Board more frequently than was the case before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the position is not -- not just that you were not automatically obliged to go but actually you were not automatically entitled to go, were you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- oh, there's just one point I want to clear up with you. So far as correspondence -- we talked about telephone calls. But so far as written communications were concerned as between the Main Board and Executive Board on the one hand and your local municipality board on the other, is it right that you -- you really don't have any real idea of the frequency of such correspondence during the period June 1991 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I personally did not jot down telephone conversations and telephone interventions and messages, but it's customary that the materials from the Main Board and the Executive Board which relate to the Municipal Boards were forwarded by mail to us, and we would inform ourselves about the material at Municipal Boards. We would act in accordance with them, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that in your interview, the first one actually, at page 12 of the 207-page transcript, Mr. Mitford-Burgess said to you - it's the middle of that page - "You were in the capacity as the president of the SDS party at Ilidza. You received correspondence are from the Main Board of the SDS party at Sarajevo." And your answer was, "Normally the correspondence should be and it was, but I do not know what was the intensity of that correspondence." Do you stand by that answer, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mitford-Burgess said, "Why?" You said, "See, it was long time ago, and I can't remember now how often meetings of the Municipal Board occurred and how often we were receiving some materials or how often the Assembly had its sessions, Assembly of the city board, because that was the period after the elections that took place in 1990." Do you stand by that answer, as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, it appears to me from the context of this exchange that it begins with a period of time -- it addresses the period of time from 1990 to 1991. That's -- it seems to be reflected in the later answer, as well. But if you look up at the page that -- in the comments of the witness, he appears to be talking about the period of time from 1990 to 1991, a period of certain training for work, and then later on the answer is the limited -- the answer reflects a limited activity that took place in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that would be, no doubt, apt if it weren't for the fact that we already know from evidence, Your Honour, that this witness did not become the president of the SDS party at Ilidza until the end of June 1991, and that was what Mr. Mitford-Burgess was asking him about. It's quite true that above, in the longer answer, that was the period, but -- well, one can debate perhaps without the witness, Your Honour, what it means, but it is -- Mr. Mitford-Burgess's question was very specifically directed towards his position as the president of the SDS party, and we do know that he only took up that position in June 1991. So 1990 doesn't have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, does that sufficiently clarify the issue? The problem, of course, is that the relevant portion of the transcript of the interviews is not in evidence, so we have to work on the basis of what has been quoted now. And if you say this is sufficient, then we could proceed; if you say no, then someone would have to tender that page of the document so that we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the slightest difficulty, if it makes everybody feel more comfortable -- in fact, I do have a question in relation to the previous passage anyway. So I don't have the slightest difficulty in having that additional paragraph introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from Mr. Tieger if he finds that still the question does not properly reflect what appears in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I would only continue the quote that I truncated, that it was -- the witness's answer: "That was the period after the elections that took place in 1990, and there was no real -- some level activities as we were working in the elections," which, again, appears to be a reflection of the period of time referred to in the earlier answer. I'm not purporting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 11, 12, and 13 should be received in evidence in order to better understand this portion of the evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I -- Your Honour, with respect, I don't have any problem at all with that. They're received in evidence on the basis that it is -- the evidence is that those things were said by Mr. Prstojevic in his interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you did say -- and it's a different point, Your Honours -- picking up an answer which you gave. I better get the question, then, so we've got the context. Mr. Mitford-Burgess said, "We want to" -- something unintelligible -- "your activities" -- probably "consider" or something. "We want to look at your activities from the period of the outbreak of war in April 1992. You said that you were president of the -- the war in April of 1992. You said you were president of the SDS party. What did that involve? What were your functions?" And then you said -- your answer: "We were not used to parliamentary life and multiparty life. So the period of time from 1990 to 1991 is a period of certain training for work in the parties. There were very weak, normative acts, and I remember that at that time there was a statute for Serb Democratic Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina which prescribed municipal structure, which prescribed municipal structure of the Municipal Board and in one word, the work of the whole party. Then that's why we in Ilidza on our self-initiative tried to issue a document which we called like a main act for the work of the Municipal Board of Ilidza. That act -- that document was worked on by the end of 1991." Is -- is that document that you mentioned there in your interview, is that any document that we have seen since you began your evidence in this court this week?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document was called the statutory decision of the municipal -- of the SDS Ilidza Municipal Board, and it was completely in line in everything with the statute of the SDS party of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was drafted by a team of lawyers, economists, and so on and so forth, and it was adopted by the Municipal Board. However, that statutory decision, we didn't see at all, not when I was questioned in Sarajevo and not since I've been here in The Hague, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, if you just would have said, No, that's not a document we've seen, then you would have answered the question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you tried to issue a document which "we called like a main act," what happened to it? Did it not get the whole way to being issued or proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was adopted and published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Published how?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was adopted at the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party of Ilidza, and it was internally -- it was sent to the municipal or local boards by mail. It wasn't published in the official bulletin, and it did not have to be published in other documents. It had to be given to the Executive Board and to the Main Board of our party, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was in some way sent or transmitted, was it, to the Executive Board and the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it adopted by the Municipal Board of the SDS of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1991, as soon as it was completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this team, as you describe it, "team of lawyers, economists, and so on and so forth," that included you, did it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you one of the more active significant members of that team?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most significant ones were lawyers, who had to make sure that the document was in line with the statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many lawyers did you have working -- in the team working on this document for Ilidza SDS Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but the teams that we had for such matters usually numbered three to five people. I know that the key person was a lawyer, Mr. Slobodan Marilovic, who worked at the Sarajevo court at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber really asks itself in what way it assists to know whether there were four, three, two, or five lawyers, and then to know their names. It's really -- relevance -- you'll hardly ever hear me say "no relevance." It's low relevance, in the view of the Chamber, and the Chamber would invite you to focus on high relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mind being absolutely open about what the relevance is. We like to know the names of people so that we might be able to contact them. And therefore it certainly has relevance and would indirectly have relevance to the Trial Chamber if we were able to contact them and they were able to give evidence. It's as simple as that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say zero relevance. I said "low relevance," and I said you are invited to seek higher relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, may I say, with respect, that is of very high relevance to the Defence, and I hope Your Honour can understand exactly why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you were asked -- and this is at page 39, for everybody's reference, of the interview transcript -- you were asked about a document which has come to be known as Variants A and B. The -- you were asked when you first saw the document. This is at page 39. You said, "Practically immediately after it was brought by the end of December 1991," and you were asked by Mr. Margetts, who showed you that document. You said, "Certain structures and certain officials of the party got this document at some meeting or session in Holiday Inn, I think." And you -- you were asked by Mr. Margetts: "And who was the representative from Ilidza that received the document?" And you said, "I cannot remember really, but there was probably more of us who received it." Now, do you agree, Mr. Prstojevic, that at that point in the interview you were far from sure whether you personally had been at any such meeting in the Holiday Inn when that document was produced?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was not drafted at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, rather, distributed to us at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, nothing in my question suggested it was drafted at that meeting. I didn't, in fact, ask you to go into the question of distribution. It's clear the focus of my question was your degree of sureness or unsureness at that point in your interview about whether you yourself had been at that meeting, and that's the point which I would invite you to address in your answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said, "Certain structures" -- you were asked, "Who showed you that document?" And you said, "Certain structures and certain officials of the party got this document at some meeting or some session in Holiday Inn, I think." So that language was being applied to a meeting which you were already sure you had attended? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said before. It's a fact that I and several others from Ilidza were present at that meeting and that, at some point at the meeting, towards the end of the meeting perhaps, was distributed to us. We each received one copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 40 of that interview - and it was later the same day, the 25th of November - you were asked by Mr. Margetts, about ten lines down: "Mr. Prstojevic, if you could proceed with the explanation of who received that document, in what circumstances they received it, and what instructions accompanied the receipt of that document." And you said, "See, I think that this document was being received at one session, one meeting, maybe of the Main Board in Holiday Inn. By all means in that meeting, the members of the Main Board had to be present, I think presidents of Municipal Boards and the highest officials of municipalities. In this case, president of the Executive Board and the secretary of the Municipal Assembly and maybe somebody else from the municipal officials." Now, first of all, you were not a member of the Main Board, were you, at that time, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not have to be present.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an invitation to attend the meeting, and therefore I was duty-bound to attend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember, do you, that you specifically received an invitation to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do because that was the reason why I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, the same page, page 40, Mr. Mitford-Burgess: "Did you attend this meeting at the Holiday Inn when this document was disseminated?" Your answer: "I think I was, but I don't know who got this document." Mr. Prstojevic, when you are sure you've attended a meeting, do you normally answer a question with "I think I was," as opposed to just "yes"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you're saying, but the fact is I was present, regardless of how I termed my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the issue of the presence of the witness at that meeting has been sufficiently dealt with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the foot of page 41 of the same interview, you said, "See" -- well, I'll give the lead-in of the question so we get the context. Mr. Margetts said, "So what we would like you to do for us is just to describe for us" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would invite the witness to - - well, Your Honour says it's sufficiently dealt with. May I in the same way, then, as we did with those few pages earlier, may I ask for the whole of page 40, from where I started, and 41 to be admitted in the same way as -- as evidence of what he said during that meeting, and then I needn't dwell on the -- would that be satisfactory to Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40 and 41 will be received in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't recall having the same opportunity, and I trust in future that it will be extended to the Prosecution, when it's not in a position to deal with a topic in its entirety because of time constraint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- yes, we are not -- Mr. Stewart is asking specific questions on the basis of the interview, especially where the wording of the interview is of importance. Mr. Stewart has -- and I have suggested, as a matter of fact, in relation to page 12, to have that in evidence so that in order to assess the probative value of the testimony of the witness. We would at least know what the wording of the interview is with which he's confronted. It's not to say that it's the substance of it. If there would be any question you've put to the witness, Mr. Tieger, where you would feel that it would be appropriate that at least the Chamber has at its disposal in evidence, therefore, the exact wording the witness used during the interview because that was an element of your questions, then you're invited to let the Chamber know, and we'll decide about admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm obliged with the way we've dealt with that passage, which speeds things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm informed that -- you know that usually we stop at a quarter to 2.00. We could, I'm informed, take a few minutes more, but certainly not much because of duties for the transcribers. It looks as if we would not finish with this witness today, if we would give an opportunity to Mr. Krajisnik to ask some questions, if you, Mr. Tieger, would have some questions perhaps triggered by cross- examination, and we would have some questions. So I would rather first try to find out whether the witness would still be available in the beginning of next week. Mr. Prstojevic, it looks as if we cannot finish your testimony today. Would you still be available in the beginning of next week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be presumably in -- certainly not more than just on Monday. Then you have another seven minutes at this moment, Mr. Stewart, and then we will finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, then moving on into those seven minutes. You were -- Mr. Margetts said, "We also understand" -- or he talked about a meeting on the 14th of April. And then you said, "See, according to my opinion, I would have to refresh my memory a lot about this. There was some meeting, I suppose, in a Holiday Inn Hotel of the mentioned structures. This document is not in my hands. That means was not given to me but" -- well, I'll stop there. So is this the position, Mr. Prstojevic: That you are, as you indicated, sure that you were at a meeting at the Holiday Inn Hotel in Sarajevo in late December 1991, first of all? You're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I thought that aspect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. But I thought that aspect of this examination had been dealt with. I don't know if we're moving on to something else as a predicate, but -- which is what I was waiting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we are. We would have got there by now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I just -- you are sure about that? I'm giving you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I said that the presence of the witness has been sufficiently dealt with, and then, of course, we could ask him whether he was sure or whether he was perfectly sure or the that was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, for an advocate, when the Trial Chamber says, "The matter has been sufficiently dealt with," that does not tell the advocate clearly that -- what the Trial Chamber's conclusion was. Your Honour did not say to me, "The Trial Chamber has decided" -- and frankly, I'd be rather dismayed if the Trial Chamber had decided since the evidence in this case is a long way from complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard three times the witness saying clearly that he attended a meeting at that time and the meeting was referred to as the Holiday Inn meeting and that he at that moment received with others and he explained that he was specifically invited for it. The Chamber does not establish any fact at this moment, but the Chamber finds that as far as the evidence of this witness is concerned, that it has heard sufficient about a pertinent answer three times given. And what the final finding of the Chamber in this respect will be depends on the whole of the evidence presented in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the footing, the witness has said he was sure he was at the meeting; I leave it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question, Mr. Prstojevic, is this: You are clearly -- do you agree, you are not sure and you have no clear recollection about what happened about any such document - and this is the Variant A and B document - at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the discussion at that particular meeting about this specific document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall anything with any confidence relating to that document at all at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall with clarity what I've already mentioned; that one of the four of us who were there from Ilidza - and I cannot recall their names now - that we received the document and that we acted upon that document by implementing one of its phases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, is -- is this the position: That you are inferring from the fact that at some point you had this document, that it was given to one of your colleagues at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an inference; it's a fact. One of the four of us did receive the copy, and Momcilo Cencic [phoen] was, I believe, also present on one of the commmissions there. Whether it was Kezomovic [phoen], the people's hero, --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- whether it was Chencic or myself, but one of us received the copy in person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't even know who was present at that meeting from Ilidza, do you, Mr. Prstojevic, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that the persons I've indicated here were present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you were certain, why did you say, then -- and this is at page 40 of your interview, when asked by Mr. Margetts: "Who were representatives from Ilidza that attended the meeting," your answer was, "I do not know who was present, but I suppose Ljubo Bosilic [phoen], Radomir Kaseonovic [phoen], Momcilo Ceklic." Because, Mr. Prstojevic, do you agree that is a very different answer, "I do not know who was present," from saying now that you are certain that those persons were present? Do you -- do you accept yourself -- they're your words in both cases. Do you accept that is something very different?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do accept that it is different, but at that time, without any preparations, I left the manager's office to attend this interview. I had not prepared myself beforehand, and I did not have the opportunity to refresh my memory as I do have today in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said specifically, Mr. Prstojevic, that you had not prepared yourself and had not had time to prepare yourself for this evidence. That's what you told the Trial Chamber earlier this week, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in Your Honour's hands entirely on that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I would have one question for you, Mr. Prstojevic. Earlier today you said, "It is a fact that I and several others from Ilidza were present at that meeting and that at some point at the meeting, towards the end of the meeting perhaps, was distributed at the" -- so you were talking about the distribution of the document. And then you said, "We each received one copy." Whereas, now you tell us that one of you received a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I said that we each received one copy, then it was a mistake of mine because that was not the case. It must have been a slip of the tongue or maybe a misinterpretation. Every Municipal Board received a copy each. And as you see, Your Honours, the documents are numerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Prstojevic, we'd like to see you back next Monday at 9.00 in this same courtroom, and I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you are still about to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. And for the parties: Mr. Tieger, Friday is dossier day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It certainly is, Your Honour. And I'm pleased to report the submission of the following dossiers: Bijeljina, Ilijas, Prijedor, Rogatica, and Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They'll be distributed, and we'll then have a look at it and see whether there are any questions arising out of it. If there are no further urgent matters to be dealt with at this moment, we'll adjourn until next Monday, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.54 p.m.,
